entities.summary:
The Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, first commissioned in 1991, represents a significant advancement in naval warfare technology, with its design rooted in a response to the changing dynamics of global military engagements. Developed by the United States Navy, these guided missile destroyers have been pivotal in enhancing maritime security and power projection since the end of the Cold War, reflecting the strategic military priorities of the United States in the post-1980s geopolitical landscape. The class was named after Admiral Arleigh Burke, a distinguished naval officer who played critical roles in World War II and the Korean War, symbolizing a legacy of naval innovation and operational excellence.

The Arleigh Burke-class destroyers are distinguished by their Aegis Combat System, which integrates advanced radar and missile systems, enabling them to perform a wide range of missions from anti-aircraft defense to land attack. The first ship, USS Arleigh Burke (DDG-51), was launched on July 16, 1989, and has been followed by more than 60 ships in active service, making it one of the most produced classes of modern warships. The destroyers have participated in numerous operations, including the Global War on Terror and various humanitarian missions, highlighting their versatility and importance in contemporary naval operations.

The legacy of the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer extends beyond its operational capabilities; it has influenced naval design and strategy worldwide, leading to the development of advanced destroyer classes in other nations. Countries such as Japan and South Korea have adopted similar technologies and strategies, reflecting the global impact of the Burke class on naval warfare. As Admiral Burke himself stated, 'The Navy's principal duty is to support the national economy and not the other way around,' underscoring the destroyer's role in both military and economic dimensions of national security.
